```{r}
source("R/helpers.R")
set.seed(STUDENT_SEED)

location <- 0
scale <- 1
generator <- function(sample_size) {
  rcauchy(sample_size, location = location, scale = scale)
}
```

## Why this case is different

The standard Cauchy distribution has extremely heavy tails. Its ordinary mean
and variance do not exist, so there is no finite theoretical standard deviation
to insert into `sigma / sqrt(n)`. This means the usual finite-variance CLT
argument is not applicable.

This is not a technical problem with the simulation. It is the main reason the
Cauchy population is included.

## Original population

```{r}
population <- rcauchy(10000, location = location, scale = scale)
population_for_plot <- population[abs(population) <= 25]
plot_population_histogram(
  population_for_plot,
  "Cauchy population (values beyond +/-25 omitted from display)",
  "Population value"
)
```

The display is trimmed only so that a few extreme values do not make the plot
unreadable. The extreme values themselves are part of the distribution and
are not removed from the sample-mean simulations below.

## Simulation

I investigated sample sizes `n = 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, and 200`. I used
the same range as the other distributions so that the comparisons were fair.
The smaller values show the immediate effect of the heavy tails, while the
larger values test whether increasing `n` fixes the problem.

```{r}
means_by_size <- simulate_sample_means(generator)

cauchy_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(means_by_size), function(size_name) {
  means <- means_by_size[[size_name]]
  data.frame(
    sample_size = as.numeric(size_name),
    simulated_mean = mean(means),
    simulated_sd = sd(means),
    median = median(means),
    skewness = skewness(means),
    excess_kurtosis = excess_kurtosis(means),
    proportion_beyond_10 = mean(abs(means) > 10),
    row.names = NULL
  )
}))

print_summary(cauchy_table)
```

The simulated mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis can change a
lot when extreme values appear. A stable finite-variance standard-error
comparison is not available here.

## Visual evidence

```{r}
selected_sizes <- c(2, 10, 30, 200)

old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

for (sample_size in selected_sizes) {
  means <- means_by_size[[as.character(sample_size)]]
  means_for_plot <- means[abs(means) <= 25]
  hist(
    means_for_plot,
    breaks = 40,
    col = "#f4a261",
    border = "white",
    main = paste0("Cauchy means, n = ", sample_size,
                  " (display trimmed)"),
    xlab = "Sample mean"
  )
}
par(old_par)

plot_selected_qq(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Cauchy Q-Q plot")
```

The histograms are trimmed only for readability. The numerical summaries and
Q-Q plots use the simulated values, so extreme departures from the line should
be interpreted as evidence of heavy tails rather than treated as ordinary
sampling noise.

## Approximate normal decision

The Cauchy population did not behave like the other populations. Extreme
values continued to affect the sample means even when `n` became large. Since
the Cauchy distribution has no finite ordinary mean or variance, the usual CLT
standard-error formula does not apply. Therefore, I did not choose a sample
size for this distribution. My final answer is: **there is no reasonable value
of `n` under the ordinary CLT conditions**. The histograms and Q-Q plots kept
showing heavy-tail behavior, and the simulated mean, standard deviation,
skewness, and kurtosis were unstable. Because there is no finite theoretical
standard error to compare with, the usual numerical check cannot be used here.

## What surprised me

I was surprised that increasing the sample size to 200 did not make the
sample-mean distribution behave like the other populations. A few extreme
values could still have a large effect, which is exactly why the Cauchy case is
an important exception to the usual CLT discussion.
